title: Two Ways to Store a Binary Tree
quickIdea: A linked node carries two pointers; a complete tree can live in an array where the children of index i sit at 2i+1 and 2i+2, but a skewed tree then wastes exponentially many slots.
remember: Linked form: struct node { int data; struct node *left, *right; } and a pointer to the root. Two pointers per node, and a missing child is NULL.
Array form with the root at index 0: the children of index i are 2i+1 and 2i+2, and the parent of index i is (i-1)/2 in integer division.
Some texts use the root at index 1, where the children of i are 2i and 2i+1 and the parent is i/2. Both conventions are common, so read the question before computing an index.
A complete binary tree of n nodes fills indices 0 to n-1 exactly, so an array of n slots is enough and no slot is wasted.
Any other shape wastes slots: a chain of h+1 nodes needs 2^(h+1) - 1 slots, so ten nodes in a chain need 1023 slots to store ten values.
The linked form needs the same number of nodes whatever the shape, which is why it is the default for general trees; the array form wins on locality and on parent lookup, which is what a heap needs.

example.prompt: A complete binary tree holds the values 8, 4, 12, 2, 6, 10, 14, 1 in level order. Give the array, the children of the node holding 12, and the parent of the node holding 1.
example.work: Level order gives index 0 to 7: 8, 4, 12, 2, 6, 10, 14, 1. The value 12 is at index 2, so its children are at 2*2+1 = 5 and 2*2+2 = 6, holding 10 and 14. The value 1 is at index 7, so its parent is (7-1)/2 = 3, holding 2. All eight slots are used, so nothing is wasted.
example.answer: Array 8, 4, 12, 2, 6, 10, 14, 1; 12's children are 10 and 14; 1's parent is 2.

gateAngle: Array questions ask for the index arithmetic or the number of slots a shape needs. GATE has asked the 2D array address form in the same subject, so the index formula is worth having automatic; the tree version is the same idea one level up.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A binary tree of height 9 is stored in an array using the root-at-0 convention, and every node has only a right child. How many slots must the array have, and how many of them are used?
variations.why: A chain of height 9 has 10 nodes, and the rightmost node sits at index 2^10 - 2 = 1022, so the array must be 1023 long. Only the 10 chain positions hold data.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: In the root-at-0 convention, what is the index of the parent of the leftmost leaf of a perfect binary tree of height 2, and how many slots does the array need?
variations.answer: Parent index 1, and the array needs 7 slots.
variations.why: A perfect tree of height 2 has 7 nodes at indices 0 to 6, so its leaves sit at 3, 4, 5 and 6 and the leftmost is index 3. The parent of index 3 is (3-1)/2 = 1, which holds the second level's left node.

trap.what: Assuming an array of n slots always stores a binary tree of n nodes.
trap.why: The packed indexing is exact only for complete trees. For any other shape the largest index can be far beyond n-1.
trap.counterexample: A chain 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 descending to the right sits at indices 0, 2, 6, 14, so four nodes already need 15 slots, and the ten-node chain needs 1023.

check.question: In the root-at-0 convention, a node sits at index 6. What is its parent index, and which of its children indices exist in a complete tree of 10 nodes?
check.answer: Parent index 2; the left child index 13 does not exist, since the tree's indices stop at 9.
check.explanation: (6-1)/2 = 2 in integer division. The children of 6 would be 13 and 14, both past the last index 9 of a 10-node complete tree, so index 6 is a leaf.
